newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish police mount show of force for NATO summit.
newsitem.headline: Spanish police mount show of force for NATO summit.

text.p: Thousands of Spanish police, many wearing body armour and wielding machineguns, mounted a show of force on Monday to discourage attacks by ETA Basque separatist guerrillas on the eve of an historic NATO summit.

Promising an airtight security net, police sources said they were prepared for the possibility of violence by ETA and other radical groups who might target leaders attending the two-day summit, which opens on Tuesday morning.

Armoured vehicles were deployed around the city and police and Civil Guard soldiers took up positions around the U.S. embassy in Madrid. On a main street outside the compound, a gunner watched over passing traffic from a machinegun nest atop a small armoured car.

City leaders say they already have solid anti-terrorist systems in place against attacks by ETA, but officials were taking no chances as they made final security preparations for one of Spain's biggest international gatherings in years.

Police were on alert for possible retaliation by ETA for the arrests in the past week of eight alleged members of a rebel cell suspected of involvement in the kidnapping of a prison official. Civil Guards rescued the hostage on Tuesday after 532 days in captivity.
ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna issued a veiled threat after the rescue mission, saying: "After the drunkenness comes the hangover".
ETA, which stands for Basque Homeland and Freedom, has waged a 29-year campaign of violence to demand an independent Basque homeland encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.
About 800 people have been killed in the conflict, including senior public figures assassinated in the heart of Madrid and other cities.
The rebels have intensified the violence this year, killing nine people so far after a relative lull in 1996.
A force of 4,000 police and Civil Guard troops were stationed at key points around Madrid and a sprawling convention centre on the outskirts of the city where NATO leaders were meeting.
"There will be a very significant deployment because we think that an event of this character demands it," the interior ministry said in a statement issued ahead of the summit.
U.S. President Bill Clinton was flying to Madrid on Monday afternoon from the Spanish island of Majorca where he spent the weekend relaxing with his family as the guests of Spanish King Juan Carlos.
Fifteen other NATO heads of state or government and up to 28 leaders of NATO partner countries were also arriving on Monday and Tuesday.
With tight security measures expected to snarl up traffic throughout the city, police advised motorists to leave their cars at home for three days starting on Monday.
